Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, minimizing the radiation dose to one of the parotid glands with the help of IMRT (Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy) in patients with advanced head and neck cancers can indeed help prevent xerostomia, a common side effect of radiation treatment for this condition. Xerostomia is characterized by dry mouth due to reduced saliva production.

Studies have shown that using IMRT can improve the sparing of parotid glands during radiation therapy, leading to improved oral function and a lower incidence of xerostomia in some patients. The use of IMRT allows for more precise targeting of tumors while minimizing exposure to surrounding healthy tissues, including salivary glands like the parotid gland.

While the question does not explicitly ask about the dose reduction itself but rather if it can prevent xerostomia, the context suggests that reducing radiation dose to one parotid gland can help alleviate the side effect of xerostomia. This is particularly relevant for patients undergoing IMRT treatment for head and neck cancers.

In summary, the available information from healthcare Q&A matches supports the idea that minimizing the radiation dose to one parotid gland can prevent or minimize xerostomia in some patients with advanced head and neck cancers undergoing radiation therapy using IMRT.
